Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Topoisomerase VI is a chirally-selective, preferential DNA decatenase" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Cynthia Wolberger as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

Please address the points raised by the referees in the sections below.

Reviewer #1:

In current paper, McKie et al. describe single-molecule magnetic tweezer measurements to show that M. mazei topoisomerase VI relaxes DNA more effectively when acting on positively supercoiled substrates, and that it unlinks DNA catenanes (experimentally mimicked by forming braided DNAs), particularly substrates with positive crossings, even more actively. Following an established approach used to characterize the chiral discrimination of DNA by bacterial topoisomerase IV, the authors integrate the magnetic tweezer data with angular probabilities derived from computational simulations of fluctuating DNA crossings. It is established that the penchant for specific DNA crossing angles by topo VI underlies the enzyme's preference for positive crossings, and that those angles are found more frequently in braids/catenanes than in plectonemes. A combination of magnetic tweezer measurements and biochemical assays are also used to show that while topo VI is a distributive and slow relaxase, it is a more potent and processive decatenase.

McKie et al. also deduce constraints on the mechanism of topo VI, beyond the preferred crossing angle, by interpreting counterintuitive results of DNA binding and cleavage assays. The tweezer data show greater relaxation activity for positive supercoils, yet the strength of DNA binding and amount of DNA cleavage are higher for negative supercoils. The authors rule out G-segment-only binding on negative supercoils (since binding and ATPase activity on relaxed and linear DNA are poor) and instead posit that chiral preference is set at the DNA-gate opening or strand passage steps, as has been proposed for human topo II β.

The paper is well-organized and clearly written, with observations appropriately contextualized in light of previous work showing that topo VI is a DNA crossover sensor, and with respect to other type II topoisomerases and the biology of archaea and plants. While there are some suggested recommendations that can be made for clarifying certain points or shoring up some of the claims, the findings overall appear supported by the data. The work constitutes a meaningful contribution to the understanding of mechanism in topo VI and the results and interpretations are situated thoughtfully amid the existing type II topoisomerase literature.

• The authors have specified that error bars refer to standard error of the mean but haven't stated numbers or natures of replicates.

• It would be helpful to show ATPase activity data for positively supercoiled DNA as well as negative in Figure 4A.

• In the Discussion section, page 23 paragraph 2, it says that the near-90° crossing angle for braids could explain the switch from distributivity on plectonemes to processivity on braids by "promoting more stable DNA binding and efficient strand passage." This is speculative and a bit at odds with the binding on supercoils, and further raises the question as to whether there is a way to show binding strength (or unbound/bound fractions) for braids/catenanes in parallel with the data for negative supercoil binding tighter than positive. Please comment.

• Page 14 paragraph 1 (in regard to Figure 4D) states that the rate and extent of processive bursts are fairly constant over large concentration changes. However, for the rate plot, there is by eye a notable, fairly steady rate dependence (~1.5x increase for positive, ~2x increase for negative), especially in light of how the changes in Figure 6 Figure Supplement 1 C and D are described. It might be better to admit that the rates do increase slightly, but that since the burst sizes do not increase and because the dwell times decrease to some limit, it could still be concluded that the phenomena result from a single, processive enzyme rather than a concentration increase.

• Page 8, end of first paragraph. Why assume that positive crossover selection occurs following DNA cleavage? Why not just posit that the binding of negative crossovers, while favored, is also mildly inhibitory to strand passage? This would seem very analogous to topo IV. Or perhaps there is some confusion as to when preference occurs that could be cleared up in the writing?

Reviewer #2:

Diverse type II topoisomerases perform critical roles managing DNA topology in cells; all off these enzymes are capable of carrying out a duplex strand passage reaction, but different enzymes specialize in harnessing this mechanism for distinct functions such as relaxation of positive and/or negative supercoiling, introduction of negative supercoiling, or decatenation. McKie et al. set out to characterize and understand the specialization of topoisomerase VI. They make use of tools including single-molecule assays with exquisitely well-controlled substrates to build on prior structural and biochemical work and help reconcile prior reports of its weak supercoil relaxation activity with its physiological importance.

The central comparison of single-molecule activity on supercoiled vs braided DNA molecules confirms and extends prior characterization of topoisomerase VI as a weak and distributive supercoil relaxase, while simultaneously clearly establishing that braids – an analog of physiological catenanes – are much more robustly relaxed. The application of the elegant single-crossing assay (introduced by Neuman et al. in earlier work), interpreted with the help of MC and BD simulations, leads to the strongly supported finding that topoisomerase VI prefers a crossing angle slightly less than 90 degrees. The authors also obtain a very clear measurement of a modest chiral preference on both supercoiled and braided substrates, and it is satisfying that for this enzyme the optimal crossing angle alone appears sufficient to explain this preference.

It is clear that there are relatively high average rates of braid relaxation. The stronger claim of even faster processive bursting may well also be correct, but is harder to evaluate from the information presented, which does not include a detailed analysis of the limits of the step-finding procedure (from Seol and Neuman) in its specific application here, nor any extensive presentation of raw traces. Given the quite small reported processivities, small extension signals in comparison to supercoil relaxation, and burst rates that are not quite insensitive to concentration, this is a claim where the details of the analysis are important for establishing confidence.

It is striking that the preferred crossing angle is quite similar to topo IV, but the degree of preference seems much more stringent – a conclusion based on the narrow range of geometries where the authors observe activity in single-crossing assays. A stringent preference for crossing angles near 90 degrees is central to the authors' explanations of preferential activity on braids and catenanes. However, the characterization and explanation of the difference in stringency with topo IV seem underexplored quantitatively, since the authors do not discuss e.g. the raw probabilities of sampling the optimal crossing angle in the assayed geometries that did not show any measurable activity, or the limits of detectable rates in their measurements.

Overall, this work advances the field by presenting a compelling case for topo VI as an effective decatenase, helping focus attention on this activity in its physiological roles, while presenting a plausible hypothesis – a strict crossing angle preference for strand passage – uniting observations of activities on diverse substrates.

To address my comments about burst analysis, I suggest:

1. Showing steps of representative traces, together with overlaid step-finding outputs.

2. Providing details of the step-finding procedure and subsequent analysis. E.g, the legend indicates that bursts were defined as two or more cycles; at what stage was that criterion imposed? Did step-finding also find smaller bursts (e.g. 1 cycle) and then those were excluded from subsequent analysis? Were the reported burst sizes corrected to account for the detection threshold?

3. Revisiting the simulation approach that was compelling for validating results in Seol et al. For example, if you simulate a "null hypothesis" of distributive activity with the same average braid relaxation rate measured in your assay, and include realistic noise, then apply the analysis pipeline used for experiments, what comes out?

To address my comments about ingle-crossing stringency, I suggest:

1. Report directly on tethers that showed no activity; what was the simulated distribution of crossing angles for those tethers? In particular, how does the probability of sampling the preferred crossing angle compare with tethers for which activity was observed?

2. How much slower must the rates be on these "no activity detected" tethers for relaxation to not be measurable?

3. While not as elegant as the internally controlled left-right comparisons, can raw rates of relaxation be compared between different tethers and related to the simulated probabilities of observing the preferred crossing angle?

Additional questions and suggestions:

Generally the discussion of crossing angles for different substrates (braids and supercoils at difference forces, catenanes and supercoils in the absence of force) would be quantitatively improved by calculating distributions of crossing angles for these cases in a unified analysis; I recognize this is a significant simulation task and currently you reference some past work to support general claims. At minimum I would reference, consider, and discuss early work presenting distributions of juxtaposition angles, from Vologodskii and Cozzarelli (1994 and 1996), which includes simulations of weakly supercoiled DNA (1996) where the juxtapositions that occur are still broadly distributed and just starting to be asymmetric.

The biochemical decatenation assay used here and in Ref. 47 is quite striking. What can you say about how "special" topo VI is in terms of the results of that assay? Ref. 47 shows a similar result for topo II α, where catenation occurs at a lower enzyme concentration than supercoil relaxation. How about other topo II enzymes, e.g. yeast topo II, bacterial topo IV…?

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Topoisomerase VI is a chirally-selective, preferential DNA decatenase" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Philip Cole as the Senior Editor.

The manuscript has been much improved. Both referees are favorable but request that a couple of issues still be addressed, as outlined below:

Reviewer #1:

The authors have satisfactorily addressed all major comments. A couple typos still appear to have snuck through: "WaveMentrics" in Figure 1C caption, and the formatting of Weeks-Chandler potential is fixed but the Debye-Huckle is not.

Reviewer #2:

In their revision, McKie et al. have added substantial new analyses, experiments, and clarifications to their manuscript, strengthening their study while responding thoughtfully to many of the issues raised by both reviewers. I am supportive of publication in eLife, and my remaining comments are concerned with just a few points on which I feel the authors could be more complete in addressing questions from the previous round of review, without requiring additional experiments or extensive calculations.

Burst analysis for unbraiding analysis:

I previously asked that the authors show representative traces, together with overlaid step-finding outputs. This request was minimally addressed by adding the step-finding overlay to the single trace that was already included in Figure 4B. To give the reader a more representative sense of this data and analysis, I think it would be appropriate to show more traces and overlays, including under varying conditions; this could be done in a supplementary figure. The annotation and description of Figure 4B itself could also be more clear: the step-finding output appears to show three bursts, but the main text refers to the figure as showing "two rapid bursts", and the annotation and rate calculation from the text implicitly treat the relaxation as a single burst – 10 passages in 10 s for a rate of 1/s – while the burst rates (that would be extracted for tabulation in Figure 4D) from this trace must be somewhat higher than that (and higher than average, based on 4D), since much of that 10 s period is taken up with pauses; correct?

I had also requested details of the step-finding procedure – currently described with a quick reference to Seol et al. (2016) – but was perhaps insufficiently specific in this request; what choices were made for the window size, probability threshold, and criteria for false positive rejection? I further suggested validating the analysis of processivity using simulated data as was nicely done and argued for in Seol et al. The authors did not take up this suggestion, but addressed an underlying question by making a statistical argument against a distributive model in their response. A version of this argument could be included in the paper, but I think the probabilities of observing long dwells (in a distributive model) are underestimated in the authors' response, since they are based on the extracted burst rates (4D). In a distributive model, the rate that governs the dwell statistics would be equal to the average relaxation rate (4C), an unbiased measure obtained independent of the fitting procedure. (A comparison with analysis of simulated data would of course be more complete and convincing, since it also includes biasing effects of the analysis such as missed short events.) Overall, the observations of the authors do seem to support modest processivity, but I think is fair for them to caution in the text that rigorous quantification of the processive behavior will require further work and analysis – as has already been hinted at in the discussion of concentration dependence.

Distributions of crossing angles:

I agree that the analysis of crossing angle distributions previously calculated for supercoiled DNA by Vologodskii and Cozzarelli has strengthened the paper. This analysis relates to comparing positively and negatively supercoiled DNA. Additional nuance could be introduced into the discussion comparing supercoiled DNA with catenanes: the authors note that ~90° angles occur much more frequently in catenanes than in supercoiled DNA, which is certainly true for the supercoiling and catenation densities simulated in the referenced Stone et al. paper. Note however that the distribution depends on supercoiling density (Vologodskii and Cozzarelli 1996, Figure 6); for weakly supercoiled DNA, there is a broader distribution centered closer to 90°. In general, I think it is worth pointing out in the discussion (as acknowledged by the authors in their response) that quantitatively relating substrate preferences to crossing angle selection will require simulations of the various substrates under different conditions, beyond the mean crossing angle calculations and selected previously simulated distributions presented here.

claims.claim: Topo VI was initially isolated from the hyperthermophilic archaeon, Sulfolobus shibatae in 1994.

claims.claim: S. shibatae topo VI was shown to relax positive and negative supercoils, but decatenated more efficiently, with threefold less enzyme required to decatenate 0.4 μg of kinetoplast DNA than was required to relax 0.4 μg of negatively supercoiled pTZ18.

claims.claim: A. thaliana topo VI was crucial during endoreduplication.

claims.claim: Top6B was demonstrated to be extremely important for tightly coupling ATPase activity to strand passage.

claims.claim: Topo VI relaxed positive supercoils ~2–3 fold faster than negative supercoils.
claims.source: The observed DNA extension changes revealed that, on average, topo VI relaxed positive supercoils ~2–3 fold faster than negative supercoils.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claims.claim: The average relaxation rates for supercoils of either chirality increased as a function of topo VI concentration.
claims.source: We found that the average relaxation rates for supercoils of either chirality increased as a function of topo VI concentration with the data fitted to a Michaelis Menten-like equation, resulting in an apparent Kd (Kd,app) threefold lower for the relaxation of positive DNA writhe.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claims.claim: The apparent Kd for topo VI is threefold lower for the relaxation of positive DNA writhe compared to negative.
claims.source: We found that the average relaxation rates for supercoils of either chirality increased as a function of topo VI concentration with the data fitted to a Michaelis Menten-like equation, resulting in an apparent Kd (Kd,app) threefold lower for the relaxation of positive DNA writhe.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements fitted to a Michaelis-Menten-like equation.

claims.claim: The relaxation of positively and negatively supercoiled pBR322* by topo VI was completed by 6 min and 15 min, respectively.
claims.source: In line with the single-molecule relaxation assay results, the preferential relaxation on positive supercoils by topo VI is also supported by an agarose gel based approach (Figure 1D), showing that the relaxation of positively and negatively supercoiled pBR322* was completed by 6 min and 15 min, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from an agarose gel-based assay shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Each topo VI strand-passage event results in an abrupt DNA extension change of ∼100 nm, which corresponds to the resolution of a single DNA crossing.
claims.source: For topo VI, each strand-passage event is evident in the trace, as an abrupt DNA extension change of ∼100 nm, which is expected for the resolution of a single DNA crossing (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Topo VI binds and resolves a single crossing before disengaging the G-segment, indicating distributive activity.
claims.source: This provided preliminary evidence of distributive activity, as many seconds to minutes elapsed between strand-passage events, indicating that topo VI binds and resolves a single crossing before disengaging the G-segment.
claims.evidence: This inference is based on the observation of long dwell times between strand-passage events in the magnetic tweezers data.

claims.claim: The dwell time between strand-passage events as a function of plectoneme crossings was well-fitted by an inverse relationship.
claims.source: The dwell-time between strand-passage events as a function of plectoneme crossings was well-fitted by an inverse relationship, indicating that the time taken to bind a crossing and perform strand-passage was inversely proportional to the number of DNA crossings present (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The time taken for topo VI to bind a crossing and perform strand-passage was inversely proportional to the number of DNA crossings present.
claims.source: The dwell-time between strand-passage events as a function of plectoneme crossings was well-fitted by an inverse relationship, indicating that the time taken to bind a crossing and perform strand-passage was inversely proportional to the number of DNA crossings present (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This inference is based on the inverse relationship fit to the experimental data.

claims.claim: Topo VI specifically recognizes and binds DNA crossings, making each crossing along the plectoneme a potential site of activity.
claims.source: This finding further supports the distributive nature of topo VI in supercoil relaxation and cements the conclusion described in Wendorff and Berger, 2018 that topo VI specifically recognises and binds DNA crossings (Wendorff and Berger, 2018), making each crossing along the plectoneme a potential site of activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from this study and a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Topo VI's specific binding to DNA crossings within the plectoneme is in sharp contrast to topo IV, which relaxed supercoiled DNA independent of the number of crossings.
claims.source: This specific binding to DNA crossings within the plectoneme is in sharp contrast to topo IV, which relaxed supercoiled DNA independent of the number of crossings, suggesting a single binding site, hypothesised to be the plectoneme end-loop (Neuman et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This comparison is based on data from this study and a citation to previous work on topo IV.

claims.claim: The rate of ATP hydrolysis by topo VI was dramatically stimulated in the presence of negatively-supercoiled pBR322*, in comparison to either relaxed or linearised pBR322*.
claims.source: Using a radioactive ATPase assay, the rate of ATP hydrolysis was observed to be dramatically stimulated in the presence of negatively-supercoiled pBR322*, in comparison to either relaxed or linearised pBR322*, and tightly coupled to the level of DNA supercoiling, with ATP hydrolysis decreasing once the DNA was relaxed (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a radioactive ATPase assay shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: ATP hydrolysis by topo VI is tightly coupled to the level of DNA supercoiling, with ATP hydrolysis decreasing once the DNA was relaxed.
claims.source: Using a radioactive ATPase assay, the rate of ATP hydrolysis was observed to be dramatically stimulated in the presence of negatively-supercoiled pBR322*, in comparison to either relaxed or linearised pBR322*, and tightly coupled to the level of DNA supercoiling, with ATP hydrolysis decreasing once the DNA was relaxed (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a radioactive ATPase assay shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The rate of ATP hydrolysis by topo VI with positively-supercoiled DNA was ~2 fold faster than with negatively-supercoiled DNA.
claims.source: With positively-supercoiled DNA, we found that the rate of ATP hydrolysis, measured using a PK/LDH coupled assay, was ~2 fold faster than with negatively-supercoiled DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a PK/LDH coupled ATPase assay shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: DNA binding by topo VI in the absence of ATP increases with increasing levels of supercoiling.
claims.source: DNA binding by topo VI in the absence of ATP, assayed using a nitrocellulose-membrane capture technique (Litwin et al., 2015), also indicates increased topo VI binding with increasing levels of supercoiling (Figure 3C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a nitrocellulose-membrane capture assay shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: Topo VI preferentially bound negatively supercoiled DNA in the absence of ATP.
claims.source: However, whereas relaxation and ATPase activity was ~2–3 fold higher for positive writhe than negative, topo VI preferentially bound negatively supercoiled DNA in the absence of ATP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from DNA binding assays.

claims.claim: The topo VI preference for relaxing positive writhe may be facilitated during a stage post DNA binding, potentially DNA-gate opening or strand passage.
claims.source: This suggested that the topo VI preference for relaxing positive writhe may be facilitated during a stage post DNA binding, potentially DNA-gate opening or strand passage.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that binding is higher for negative supercoils but relaxation is faster for positive supercoils.

claims.claim: DNA cleavage by topo VI was enhanced on negatively-supercoiled DNA compared to positively-supercoiled DNA.
claims.source: Furthermore, the amount of DNA cleavage, as measured using an agarose gel-based assay, also indicates that negatively-supercoiled DNA supports higher levels of ADPNP-dependent cleavage by topo VI than positively-supercoiled DNA (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from an agarose gel-based cleavage assay shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The maximum rate measured for positive and negative supercoil relaxation by topo VI was 6.4 ± 0.6 and 3.5 ± 0.5 strand-passage events min–1, respectively.
claims.source: Even at high concentrations (e.g. 2 nM topo VI), the maximum rate measured for positive and negative supercoil relaxation was only 6.4 ± 0.6 and 3.5 ± 0.5 strand-passage events min–1, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claims.claim: Topo VI supercoil relaxation rates are 10–50-fold slower than rates measured for the type IIA topoisomerases, gyrase and topo IV.
claims.source: As detailed in the subsequent section, these rates are 10–50-fold slower than rates measured for the type IIA topos, gyrase and topo IV (Agarwal and Duderstadt, 2020; Basu et al., 2012; Stone et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This comparison is based on data from this study and citations to previous work on other topoisomerases.

claims.claim: The maximal topo VI ATP hydrolysis rate was ∼3 ATP min–1 during relaxation of negatively supercoiled plasmids.
claims.source: Wendorff and Berger, 2018 found the maximal topo VI ATP hydrolysis rate, using the PK/LDH assay, to be ∼3 ATP min–1 during relaxation of negatively supercoiled plasmids (Wendorff and Berger, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The ATPase rate of topo VI was determined to be ∼5 ± 0.9 ATP min–1 using a radioactive ATPase assay.
claims.source: Here, the ATPase rate was determined to be ∼5 ± 0.9 ATP min–1, using a radioactive ATPase assay (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a radioactive ATPase assay shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The braid was relaxed by topo VI in three rapid bursts, at an average rate of ~0.5 strand-passage event s–1.
claims.source: In Figure 4B, the example trace of braided DNA relaxation by 0.1 nM topo VI (0.5 pN), demonstrates that the braid was relaxed in three rapid bursts, at an average rate of ~0.5 strand-passage event s–1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The rate of braid unlinking by topo VI increased ~5 fold above that of supercoil relaxation.
claims.source: however, even on average the rate of braid unlinking measured over a range of topo VI concentrations (0.05–0.9 nM) increased ~5 fold above that of supercoil relaxation (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: 0.5 nM topo VI relaxed positive supercoils at a rate of 3.5 ± 0.8 strand-passage events min–1, and positive braids at a rate of 18.9 ± 2.3 strand-passage events min–1.
claims.source: For example, 0.5 nM topo VI relaxed positive supercoils at a rate of 3.5 ± 0.8 strand-passage events min–1, and positive braids at a rate of 18.9 ± 2.3 strand-passage events min–1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claims.claim: Topo VI exhibited robust unlinking activity at concentrations ∼10-fold lower than was achievable in supercoil relaxation.
claims.source: Moreover, topo VI exhibited robust unlinking activity at concentrations ∼10-fold lower than was achievable in supercoil relaxation, and with a limited processivity, passing consecutive T-segments while remaining bound to the initial G-segment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claims.claim: Rates for topo VI processive activity approach ~0.8 strand-passage events s–1 on average during positive braid unlinking using 0.9 nM topo VI.
claims.source: Rates for topo VI processive activity (dwell times between events not included in the average) approach ~0.8 strand-passage events s–1 on average (during positive braid unlinking using 0.9 nM topo VI) (Figure 4D)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The processive rate of topo VI on braids is ~10 fold higher than the rate of positive supercoil relaxation at comparable topo VI concentrations.
claims.source: which is ~10 fold higher than the rate of positive supercoil relaxation at comparable topo VI concentrations (~0.08 strand-passage events s–1 using 1 nM topo VI).
claims.evidence: This comparison is based on experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claims.claim: When topo VI activities were assayed using a singly-catenated, supercoiled DNA substrate, the decatenation reaction occurred at topo VI concentrations 10-fold lower than for supercoil relaxation.
claims.source: In line with this, when topo VI activities were assayed using a singly-catenated, supercoiled DNA substrate, the decatenation reaction (Figure 5, left-hand agarose gel) occurred at topo VI concentrations 10-fold lower than for supercoil relaxation (Figure 5, right-hand agarose gel).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from agarose gel-based assays shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The rate of braid unlinking by topo VI is on par with those of other type IIA topoisomerases on their preferred substrates.
claims.source: Overall, the rate of braid unlinking by topo VI is on par with those of other type IIA topos on their preferred substrates.
claims.evidence: This comparison is based on data from this study and citations to previous work on other topoisomerases.

claims.claim: E. coli DNA gyrase showed one strand-passage event s–1 using a rotor bead tracking technique.
claims.source: For instance, E. coli DNA gyrase, measured using a rotor bead tracking technique, showed one strand-passage event s–1 (Basu et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: E. coli DNA gyrase showed 1.26 strand-passage events s–1 using magnetic tweezers.
claims.source: or using magnetic tweezers, 1.26 strand-passage events s–1 (Agarwal and Duderstadt, 2020)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: E. coli topo IV was demonstrated to relax positively supercoiled DNA at 2.5 strand-passage events s–1.
claims.source: and E. coli topo IV was demonstrated to relax positively supercoiled DNA at 2.5 strand-passage events s–1 (Stone et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The average unlinking rates of topo VI at concentrations ranging from 0.05 to 0.9 nM were well described by a Michaelis-Menten-like equation, providing Vmax values of 21.4 ± 0.5 and 10.9 ± 1.3 strand-passage events min–1, and Kd,app of 67 ± 7 and 164 ± 72 pM, for the unlinking of positive and negative braids respectively.
claims.source: The average unlinking rates (including dwell times between short processive bursts of activity) of topo VI at concentrations ranging from 0.05 to 0.9 nM were well described by a Michaelis-Menten-like equation, providing Vmax values of 21.4 ± 0.5 and 10.9 ± 1.3 strand-passage events min–1, and Kd,app of 67 ± 7 and 164 ± 72 pM, for the unlinking of positive and negative braids respectively (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 4C, fitted to a Michaelis-Menten-like equation.

claims.claim: The Vmax for braid unlinking is ~2 fold higher, and the Kd,app ~2.5 fold lower, for positive-braid unlinking in comparison with negative.
claims.source: The chiral preference remains, with the Vmax ~2 fold higher, and the Kd,app ~2.5 fold lower, for positive-braid unlinking in comparison with negative.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claims.claim: The chiral selection by topo VI potentially occurs after G-segment binding and cleavage, during DNA-gate opening and/or strand passage.
claims.source: Based on DNA binding and cleavage experiments (Figure 3C–E), the chiral selection potentially occurs after G-segment binding and cleavage as topo VI exhibits tighter binding and higher levels of cleavage in the presence of negative writhe than positive. This suggests that DNA-gate opening and/or strand passage is sensitive to the crossing angle, with a preference for angles more commonly found in positive writhe.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data from DNA binding and cleavage assays shown in Figure 3C-E.

claims.claim: The burst activity of topo VI on braids is due to processive unlinking by a single enzyme.
claims.source: While the processive rate modestly increased over large changes in topo VI concentration (~1.5 fold increase for positive, ~2fold increase for negative) (Figure 4D), the size of the processive bursts remained constant (Figure 4E) and the duration of the dwell times between events decreased to a minimum (Figure 4F). Together these results support the hypothesis that the burst activity is due to processive unlinking by a single enzyme.
claims.evidence: This inference is based on the concentration dependence of the processive rate, burst size, and dwell times shown in Figures 4D-F.

claims.claim: The experimental average step-sizes, probabilities of processive bursts, and average dwell times between relaxation events are substantially larger than the values from simulations of perfectly distributive braid relaxation.
claims.source: The experimental average step-sizes, probabilities of processive bursts, and average dwell times between relaxation events, are substantially larger than the values from the simulations analysed in with the same t-test step fitting routine (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3), consistent with a model in which topo VI relaxes braided DNA in short processive bursts between which the enzyme dissociates.
claims.evidence: This comparison is based on experimental data and simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claims.claim: Topo VI does not bind well to the G-segment alone.
claims.source: DNA binding and ATPase experiments show that topo VI inefficiently binds linear DNA, and the presence of this substrate does not greatly stimulate ATPase activity, indicating that topo VI does not bind well to the G-segment alone.
claims.evidence: This inference is based on experimental data from DNA binding and ATPase assays.

claims.claim: During the topo VI strand-passage reaction there is competition between the capture and passage of a T-segment at the correct geometry and the rate of topo VI dissociation from the DNA.
claims.source: This suggests that during the topo VI strand-passage reaction there is competition between the capture and passage of a T-segment at the correct geometry and the rate of topo VI dissociation from the DNA, with the former likely being accelerated in the case of DNA braids.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed differences in activity between braids and supercoils.

claims.claim: DNA crossing-angles in braids were closer to 90° than those in supercoils.
claims.source: Calculations of the average braid and supercoil angles as a function of force, corresponding to the experimental configurations of DNA length, buffer conditions, and spacing between braided DNA molecules, suggest that DNA crossing-angles in braids were closer to 90° than those in supercoils (Figure 6)
claims.evidence: This claim is based on calculations shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The DNA crossing angle may be the critical geometric factor promoting DNA unlinking by topo VI.
claims.source: and that this may be the critical geometric factor promoting DNA unlinking by topo VI.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the calculated crossing angles and observed activity differences.

claims.claim: With increasing force, the average rate of braid unlinking by topo VI drops significantly for both positive and negative writhe.
claims.source: With increasing force, the average rate of braid unlinking drops significantly (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), for both positive and negative writhe, mainly through an increase in dwell times between events with increasing force, although there is also a slight decrease in the rate and extent of the processive bursts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The supercoil relaxation rate of topo VI initially increased as the force was increased, but then rapidly decreased at higher forces.
claims.source: This interpretation is bolstered by the supercoil relaxation rate of topo VI as a function of force; the rate initially increased as the force was increased, but then rapidly decreased at higher forces ( >1 pN for positive and >0.6 pN for negative).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from magnetic tweezers measurements.

claims.claim: The characteristic unlinking time for positive crossings (τL) was 8.4 ± 1.4 s, which was 4.7-fold faster than that of negative crossings (τR) (43.8 ± 6.9 s).
claims.source: In agreement with results from DNA braids and supercoils, the characteristic unlinking time from the fitting on positive crossings (τL) for the particular braid assayed in Figure 6 was 8.4 ± 1.4 s, which was 4.7-fold faster than that of negative crossings (τR) (43.8 ± 6.9 s), suggesting that a positive crossing geometry facilitates topo VI activity through the higher probability of forming the preferred crossing angle (Figure 7C).

results.result: M. mazei topo VI is a slow, chirally-selective, and highly distributive DNA relaxase that preferentially relaxes positive supercoils 2-3 fold faster than negative supercoils, with an apparent Kd threefold lower for positive DNA writhe.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C38-C43, and C87 collectively demonstrate through single-molecule magnetic tweezers measurements (Figures 1-2) and ensemble biochemistry (Figure 1D) that topo VI relaxes positive supercoils faster than negative supercoils with quantified kinetic parameters. The distributive nature is evidenced by long dwell times between strand-passage events (C42-C43). The data are internally consistent and supported by multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: Topo VI functions as a DNA crossing sensor, with strand-passage rate inversely proportional to the number of DNA crossings present in the plectoneme, binding the G- and T-segments simultaneously rather than sequentially.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by experimental data showing inverse relationship between dwell time and crossing number (Figure 2C). Claims C96-C97 provide additional evidence from ATPase and binding assays (Figure 3) that topo VI recognizes DNA crossings. This contrasts with topo IV behavior (C47), strengthening the conclusion. The mechanistic model is well-supported by converging lines of evidence.

results.result: Topo VI demonstrates a significant increase in ATPase activity, DNA binding, and rate of strand passage with increasing DNA writhe, with ATP hydrolysis tightly coupled to supercoiling levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C48-C51, C98-C99 are supported by multiple experimental approaches including radioactive ATPase assays (Figure 3A), PK/LDH coupled assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and nitrocellulose-membrane capture assays (Figure 3C-D). The data consistently show writhe-dependent stimulation of topo VI activity across different assay types, providing strong convergent evidence.

results.result: Chiral selection by topo VI does not occur at the initial DNA binding step but potentially during DNA-gate opening and/or strand passage, as topo VI preferentially binds and cleaves negatively supercoiled DNA despite faster relaxation of positive supercoils.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 and C95 are supported by experimental data from binding assays (Figure 3C-D) and cleavage assays (Figure 3E) showing enhanced binding and cleavage on negative supercoils. Claims C53, C72, and C101 provide logical inferences from these observations. The apparent paradox between binding preference and activity preference is acknowledged and mechanistically interpreted, though the exact step remains to be definitively determined.

results.result: Topo VI activity increases approximately 10-fold on braided DNA compared to supercoiled DNA, with processive burst rates approaching ~0.8 strand-passage events s⁻¹, comparable to type IIA topoisomerases on their preferred substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 and C88 are supported by extensive magnetic tweezers data (Figures 4B-D) showing dramatically increased activity on braids. The ~10-fold increase is quantified across multiple topo VI concentrations. Comparison to type IIA topoisomerases (C66-C69) provides important context. The data are internally consistent and well-documented.

results.result: Topo VI preferentially decatenates singly-catenated DNA at concentrations 10-fold lower than required for supercoil relaxation, with braid unlinking rates comparable to type IIA topoisomerases on their preferred substrates.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by agarose gel data (Figure 5) showing decatenation at 10-fold lower concentrations than relaxation. Claims C66-C69 provide comparative context with other topoisomerases from cited literature. Claim C135 extends this to singly-catenated substrates. The convergent evidence from multiple substrate types strengthens the conclusion of preferential decatenation activity.

results.result: The burst activity of topo VI on braids is due to processive unlinking by a single enzyme, with Vmax ~2-fold higher and Kd,app ~2.5-fold lower for positive braids compared to negative braids.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 provide quantitative kinetic parameters from Michaelis-Menten fitting (Figure 4C). Claims C73-C74 establish processivity through concentration-dependence analysis (Figures 4D-F) and comparison with simulations of distributive activity (Figure 4—figure supplements 2-3). The experimental data significantly exceed simulated distributive behavior, supporting the processivity model.

results.result: DNA crossing angles in braids are closer to 90° than in supercoils, and this geometric difference is the critical factor promoting efficient DNA unlinking by topo VI through facilitated T-segment capture.
results.evaluation: Claim C77 is supported by calculations shown in Figure 6. Claims C78, C103, C105, and C113 provide mechanistic interpretations linking crossing angle to activity. Claim C111 shows force-dependent changes in crossing angles correlate with activity changes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The convergent evidence from calculations, activity measurements, and force-dependence studies supports the crossing angle model.

results.result: Force-dependent studies reveal that DNA crossing angle, rather than twist, is the primary determinant of topo VI activity, with twist playing only a secondary role at higher forces.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 and C110 document force-dependent activity changes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Claims C106-C109 analyze the role of twist versus crossing angle. The observation that twist changes are minimal at low force (C106) but activity changes are substantial supports the crossing angle model. The biphasic force-dependence of supercoil relaxation (C80, C108) is consistent with competing effects of crossing angle optimization and force-dependent inhibition.

results.result: The preferred DNA-crossing angle for topo VI is 87.4-87.8° (±0.4°), determined through single-crossing assays combined with Monte Carlo and Brownian Dynamics simulations, similar to the 85.5° preference of topo IV.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 present the primary experimental determination of preferred crossing angle from single-crossing assays (Figure 7C) combined with simulations (Figure 8C-D). Claim C83 provides independent validation using ATPase data and MC simulations (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), yielding 83-87°. Claim C84 provides comparative context with topo IV. The convergence of multiple independent approaches (two simulation methods, two experimental approaches) strongly supports the ~87.5° value.

results.result: Topo VI exhibits stricter geometric selectivity than topo IV, unable to unlink DNA crossings with imposed angles below 77°, whereas topo IV can act on crossings as acute as 50°.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is supported by experimental data from single-crossing assays (Figure 8—figure supplement 2) showing no activity below 77°. Claim C86 provides comparative data from cited literature on topo IV. This difference in geometric tolerance is an important functional distinction between the two enzymes and is well-documented experimentally.

results.result: Topo VI has evolved an intrinsic preference for unknotting and decatenation of interlinked chromosomes through preferential recognition of DNA crossings near 90°, which appear more frequently in catenanes than supercoils, making it a preferential decatenase that disfavors supercoil relaxation.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C89, and C90 represent the main conclusions of the manuscript, integrating findings from crossing angle determination (C82), activity comparisons (C88), and geometric analysis (C77, C89). The conclusion is supported by: (1) quantified 87.5° preference, (2) 10-fold activity increase on braids vs supercoils, (3) calculations showing braids have angles closer to 90° than supercoils, and (4) strict geometric selectivity (C85). The convergent evidence strongly supports this evolutionary/functional interpretation.

results.result: The maximum rate of supercoil relaxation by topo VI is 6.4±0.6 (positive) and 3.5±0.5 (negative) strand-passage events min⁻¹, which is 10-50-fold slower than type IIA topoisomerases, with ATPase rates of ~3-5 ATP min⁻¹.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 provide quantitative rate measurements from magnetic tweezers (C55) and ATPase assays (C57-C58), with comparisons to type IIA topoisomerases (C56). The rates are internally consistent (2 ATP per strand passage yields ~1.5-3.5 events min⁻¹ from 3-5 ATP min⁻¹). Multiple measurement approaches converge on similar values, supporting the conclusion of slow relaxation activity.

results.result: The 2-3-fold preference of topo VI for positive writhe, while significant, is modest compared to topo IV's 20-fold preference, and may prevent interference with DNA gyrase activity in M. mazei or support relief of replication-induced torsional strain.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 accurately compares the magnitude of chiral preference between topo VI and topo IV based on experimental data. However, claims C93-C94 are speculative inferences about in vivo implications without direct experimental support. While the speculation is reasonable given that M. mazei encodes DNA gyrase (C92, established knowledge), these functional interpretations require in vivo validation. The chiral preference is well-established, but its physiological significance remains uncertain.

results.result: During strand-passage, there is kinetic competition between T-segment capture at the correct geometry and topo VI dissociation from the G-segment, with processivity requiring continued G-segment binding after T-segment passage.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are inferences from DNA binding and ATPase data showing poor binding to linear DNA. Claims C104 and C112 provide mechanistic interpretation of the processivity observations on braids. While these are mechanistic inferences rather than direct observations, they are well-supported by the experimental data showing: (1) poor binding to linear DNA, (2) writhe-dependent activity, (3) concentration-independent burst size, and (4) concentration-dependent dwell times. The model is logically consistent with all observations.

results.result: Domains within Top6B are critical for T-segment recognition and coupling to G-segment scission, with structural precedent from topo IIβ suggesting T-segment transfer occurs in left-handed orientation.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is supported by citation to previous work (Wendorff and Berger, 2018). Claim C102 provides structural context from topo IIβ studies. These are established findings from prior work that provide mechanistic context for the current results. While not new findings from this study, they are accurately cited and relevant to the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: The decrease in supercoil relaxation rate at high force could be due to changes in twist preventing DNA binding/cleavage, or inhibition of force-sensitive steps like G-segment bending or gate closure.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 present alternative speculative explanations for the observed force-dependent decrease in activity at high force. While the experimental observation of decreased activity is well-documented (C80), the mechanistic explanation remains uncertain. The manuscript acknowledges this uncertainty by presenting multiple possibilities. Additional experiments would be needed to distinguish among these mechanisms.

results.result: M. mazei topo VI is an extremely inefficient DNA relaxase, raising questions about how archaea lacking DNA gyrase and efficient type I relaxases relieve torsional stress, though topo VI in such organisms may have evolved more efficient relaxation activity.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 is supported by data from this study and previous work. Claims C125-C130 discuss implications for archaeal biology, combining established knowledge about archaeal topoisomerase distribution (C120-C122, C126-C127) with speculation about evolutionary adaptation (C128). The inefficiency of M. mazei topo VI as a relaxase is well-established (C124), but the broader implications for archaeal biology (C125, C128) remain speculative pending studies of topo VI from other archaeal species.

results.result: Topo VI's main in vivo role may be precatenane removal during or after replication, potentially through unlinking of precatenanes formed by replication fork swiveling, with partial processivity providing utility for rapid precatenane removal.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C134 are speculative inferences about potential in vivo roles of topo VI. While the speculation is informed by the experimental findings of preferential decatenation and partial processivity, and by knowledge of fork swiveling in other organisms (C132, supported by citations), these remain hypotheses requiring in vivo validation. The manuscript appropriately presents these as possibilities rather than established facts.

results.result: The preferential decatenation activity of topo VI may explain its indispensability during endoreduplication in A. thaliana, where it could decatenate the genome unhindered while other topoisomerases are occupied with relieving transcription- and replication-induced supercoiling.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C142 accurately cite established findings about topo VI's role in plant endoreduplication. Claims C143-C144 present a speculative model to explain topo VI's indispensability based on the preferential decatenation activity demonstrated in this study. While this is a plausible and well-reasoned hypothesis that integrates the current findings with prior knowledge, it remains speculative (as acknowledged in C145). The model requires experimental validation in plant systems to determine if this is indeed the mechanism underlying topo VI's essentiality in endoreduplication.

results.result: Background information on topoisomerases, their classification, mechanisms, biological roles, and the distribution and properties of topo VI across different organisms.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1, C5-C37, C116-C123, C136) constitute background information drawn from established knowledge and cited literature. They provide essential context for the study but are not new findings. The claims are well-supported by appropriate citations and represent accurate summaries of prior work. They establish the scientific foundation and motivation for the current study.
